subtype_info: Norwegian (crusted) scabies in a child with MALT1 deficiency
title: A horse or a zebra? Unusual manifestations of common cutaneous infections in primary immunodeficiency pediatric patients
case_text:
A 3.2-year-old male was born to consanguineous parents (first cousins) of Arab origin. A male brother died at age 1.5 years from an undiagnosed condition causing fever and abscesses. A cousin was diagnosed with mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma translocation protein 1 (MALT1 deficiency). The patient had three unaffected brothers.
From the age of 5 months, the patient had recurrent episodes of fevers, sinopulmonary infections, and diarrhea. In addition, he suffered from speech delay, poor weight gain, and failure to thrive with colitis diagnosed per colonoscopy.
The initial immunologic investigation revealed leukocytosis (26.7 K/mul) with lymphocytosis (16.5 K/mul). Immunophenotyping of lymphocytes showed a normal representation of T, B, and NK cells. The result of the lymphocyte proliferation test was normal following stimulation with PHA and IL-2 but markedly reduced following stimulation with anti-CD3. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) demonstrated decreased IL-2 expression following stimulation with Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and ionomycin. TREC levels were within normal ranges.
A novel homozygous MALT1 missense mutation (c.1799T > A; p. I600N) was identified by using WES.
The diagnosis was MALT1 deficiency.
The patient was treated with monthly IVIG, prednisone, azithromycin, TMP-SMX, itraconazole, salazopyrin, and inhalations. An identical haploid transplantation from the mother was planned.
At 11 months, he presented with seborrheic dermatitis and diffuse depigmented macules on the face, trunk, and extremities, diagnosed as vitiligo, which progressed to a widespread distribution including his face, trunk, and extremities. At 12 months, he presented with severe dermatitis; he was treated chronically with topical betamethasone with eventual systemic side effects of the suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and hirsutism.
At the age of 3 years, he developed an itchy recurrent erythematous papular crusted rash involving the scalp, face, trunk, palms, and soles.
Skin biopsy from a crusted papule on the left lower back showed psoriasiform dermatitis. No parasites were seen, but due to a high clinical suspicion, scabies infection was suspected.
The rash was treated with permethrin 5% cream, including the patient's close providers, with improvement but recurrence. A few courses of permethrin were given, with only partial response. Then, he was treated with sulfur 10% ointment and a single dose of oral ivermectin of 200 mug/kg. Rash recurred and progressed to thick hyperkeratotic plaques on the extremities, palms, and soles (Figure 3A,B). Scraping from the keratotic skin lesions was positive for Sarcoptes scabies, and Norwegian scabies was diagnosed. Of note, his caretakers had a complete response to the treatment but were reinfected. Two courses of ivermectin 400 mug/kg were given 10 days apart with intense keratolytic treatment of sulfur 10% and salicylic acid without marked improvement.
MALT1-deficient patients showed defective signaling characterized by impaired NFkappaB activation and IL-2 secretion, and MALT1-deficient patients exhibited reduced regulatory T cells (Tregs) and T helper 17 (TH17) cells. Only several cases of MALT1 deficiency have been reported to date.
Patients with MALT1 deficiency have been characterized by a combination of recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. Notably, sepsis and meningitis were the most common severe infections. Severe scabies infection was not previously reported. MALT1 is required for the generation of TH17 cells, and low levels of Th17 cells were found in MALT1-deficient patients. However, crusted scabies is associated with TH2-skewed immune reaction and increased and not decreased production of Th17 cytokines. Therefore, the etiopathology of resistant crusted scabies in these patients remains to be studied.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Scabies
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Norwegian (crusted) scabies in a child with MALT1 deficiency
